speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to a question raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on June 9 regarding an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press to 66968-9-302
Inquiries of the Ministry the effect that customs officers at the port of Boissevain, Manitoba, are obliged for financial reasons to send their children to school in North Dakota, I actually had in mind another article appearing in the same paper. I answered in part and said I would obtain further information, and I wish now to clarify the matter by referring to the article to which he had reference.
The facts of this case are that the situation is not as represented. Authority had been granted by the department, with the concurrence of treasury board, to pay a car mileage allowance to the officer for the transportation of his children to and from the school at Horton, Manitoba, a distance of 9 miles. The officer, however, made arrangements to send his children to school at Dunseith, North Dakota, a distance of 13 miles from the international border.
The reasons given by the officer were that the road to Horton was hilly and heavily wooded, thus causing hazardous driving conditions; that the school board at Horton classified the children as non-residents, resulting in the officer having to pay tuition fees; also that Horton, being a rural school, taught only grades 1 to 7, which would result in the officer's eldest child having to attend school at Boissevain with the resultant tuition fees charged non-residents, as well as board and lodging. Furthermore, the North Dakota school bus proceeds to the border each morning and returns each evening, making it very convenient for the children as well as the parents.
The customs buildings and residences are located in the Turtle mountain forest reserve and are not included within a municipality. Consequently the officers are not required to pay taxes but pay rental to the department, amounting to $30 or $40 per month, depending on the type of house in which each officer lives.
The department makes every effort not to place officers with young families at isolated border offices, but when it is realized that we have 125 offices located along the international boundary it will be appreciated that it is not always possible to arrange this, having regard to the competitive system of filling positions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY IN COUNTY OF GATINEAU
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members will notice that this resolution is preceding the introduction of a measure to amend the schedule to the Prime Minister's Residence Act to bring certain property in the township of Eardley, Gatineau county, in the province of Quebec, within the scope of the act. As the Prime Minister's act was originally passed it contained in the schedule only one property, namely the house on Sussex street in the city of Ottawa. The bill which will follow this resolution merely adds to the schedule the property in the Gatineau hills which is ordinarily referred to as the Harrington lake residence.
It will be remembered that about three weeks ago the hon. member for Kootenay West asked a question on the orders of the day in the following terms:
In view of the general concern that the historic and beautiful Harrington lake residence and property be preserved and used to the best advantage, will the government recognize this concern and interest by the introduction of legislation that will establish this property as an official government country residence for use by the Prime Minister, his distinguished guests and other appropriate persons?
To that question I replied as follows:
I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. The suggestion he makes will be given serious consideration by the government. and should it be the wish generally of hon.

members that such a course be followed I should think legislation could be introduced at this session.
I mentioned this proviso because legislation of this kind is not the type that any government wishes to introduce, and in particular that no prime minister wishes to have introduced, unless members are agreed that such steps should be taken. I remember the reaction of Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent when the Prime Minister's Residence Act was introduced originally, and it was just the same as the reaction of the present Prime Minister to this proposed amendment.
These men, in a position of great responsibility, think of themselves last. If it were not the wish of the house generally to have the amendment which I am moving today passed, the government would not, of course, proceed with the measure. May I hasten to add that the other members of the cabinet, and I am sure the members of the last cabinet, feel very keenly that this measure is appropriate and, as a matter of fact, is badly needed in order to help ease the burdens of whoever may happen to be the prime minister of this nation.
The property which will be placed in the schedule if the bill carries is not the whole of the Harrington lake property, but merely 13.4 acres with the house which is on that particular portion. This property is part of a much larger property consisting of some 4,286 acres which was purchased by the federal district commission in 1951 as part of a program for the acquisition of property for the Gatineau national park. The 4,286 acres were jointly owned by Colonel C. M. Edwards and Hon. W. D. Herridge and included, the Edwards home, which is on the property now being included in the schedule, and also the Herridge home, and two farms which will remain under the administration of the national capital commission. I should like to make that clear that all the 4,286 acres, with the exception of the 13.4 acres which would be placed in the schedule to the act will remain the property of, and under the sole jurisdiction of, the national capital commission.
There has been some suggestion that the intention was to take the whole 4,286 acres and restrict anyone from fishing in Harrington lake, and a lot of such rumours, but such is not the case. All that is being done is to place the house, together with the surrounding grounds, totalling 13.4 acres in the schedule to the Prime Minister's Residence Act. The home would be available for the use of the prime minister in the summer months and also for the entertainment of distinguished guests visiting this country. Hon. members will recall that last year Her

Royal Highness Princess Margaret, during her visit to Ottawa, spent a very happy time at this residence on the shore of Harrington lake. I am sure that from time to time there will be other distinguished guests coming to Ottawa who could be entertained there during the warm summer weather.
In the course of my negotiations with members of the other parties someone made the suggestion that perhaps the leader of the opposition could have the use of the house for one day a week; and the house leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Laurier, thought he might have the use of it once very two weeks. I wondered where that left the house leader on the government side, and thought he perhaps might be able to use it once every three weeks.
In any event, indication was given from both the opposition parties that they were heartily in favour of a measure of this kind being introduced; and because of that understanding, and of the original suggestion by the hon. member for Kootenay West, I place this resolution before the committee this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to express the support of this group for this measure, which provides a most fitting and appropriate use for certain property owned by the government of Canada, namely Harrington lodge and approximately 13 acres of land. Before proceeding I must say that I was extremely pleased to hear the explanation by the Minister of Public Works concerning this measure, and was pleased to hear him scotch the various rumours that have prevailed largely because of one vivid imagination projected through a pen onto paper.
The act to provide an official residence for the prime minister of Canada was given unanimous approval by the House of Commons on January 18, 1950. At that time Mr. Cold-well, the leader of the C.C.F. group, as reported at page 3345 of Hansard of that year, said:
I think our country is doing the proper thing, in conformity with what other countries have done, in providing the first citizen of this country with a residence in which he may receive distinguished guests from at home and abroad.
I might say on this occasion, Mr. Chairman, that we in this group think our country is doing the proper thing, having a knowledge of all the circumstances, in providing Harrington lodge as an official country residence for the present and future prime ministers of Canada.
The prime ministers of Great Britain have long enjoyed an official residence and an official country residence since 1921. I might say that so long as we follow in principle the precedents, the practices and the customs of the mother of parliaments we shall not

Prime Minister's Residence Act go very far astray in this parliament. With respect to our prime minister's residence in Canada, public response and experience have proven this was a wise decision.
The whole world knows No. 10 Downing street in London. Every morning one can find the Londoner, his country cousins and overseas visitors from other parts of the commonwealth and various parts of the world gathered in front of No. 10 to witness the departure of the prime minister for the House of Commons, or for his office when the House of Commons is not in session. I should like to say that in performing this daily ritual these people are using the loom of sentiment to weave the tapestry of national strength. No. 24 Sussex drive in Ottawa is the Canadian No. 10 Downing street.
During the first world war the prime ministers of Great Britain found it increasingly necessary to leave London and find refuge in the country homes of their friends on numerous occasions. On that account the need for an official country residence for the prime minister under the trying conditions of political life in modern circumstances was increasingly recognized.
This need was met by the gift to the nation in 1921 by Lord and Lady Lee of Chequers Court in Buckinghamshire, to be used as the official residence for the prime ministers of Great Britain forever. I am going to read the beautiful inscription that was placed on the front of that residence, because I am very interested in this sort of thing. The following gracious inscription commemorating this munificent gift is found on the front wall of Chequers Court:
"This house of peace and ancient memories Was given to England as a thank-offering For her deliverance in the great war, 1914-1918, And as a place of rest and recreation For her prime ministers forever."
Since that time Liberal, Conservative and Labour prime ministers have found rest and solace in that beautiful residence during times of stress and strain.
One former prime minister of Canada, namely Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, had his Kingsmere; another former prime minister, namely Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, enjoyed his Quebec retreat. We believe, as apparently do all members of the House of Commons, that the : time is now ripe for Canada-with a knowledge of all the circumstances and the availability of this property -to provide an official country residence for Canada's prime ministers and their distinguished guqsts. This Harrington lake property, situated among woods and hear water and within a reasonable distance of Ottawa; will provide [Mr. Herridge.l
a most suitable retreat for Canada's prime ministers and their distinguished guests forever. From my personal experience since coming to Ottawa, particularly during the hot and humid days of an Ottawa summer, I might say as someone has said-I cannot recollect at the moment who it was-that at times all human beings, particularly those with heavy responsibilities to their fellow men, need the opportunity to witness the resonant far listening dawn, to enjoy the honey light of noon through leaf-laced greenery, to listen to the sounding silence of forest solitude.
Mr. Chairman, Harrington Lodge provides this opportunity. It belongs to the nation. We are pleased to know it is going to be used to the best advantage. Not only the members of the House of Commons in all parties but other people in Canada have the same opinion. I want to quote in part from an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of June 11 which I thought was most appropriate. This is what was said in this editorial on this question:
Summer Home for Prime Minister
The use of Harrington Lodge as a summer residence by Canada's prime ministers is now in prospect. A move to convert to that purpose should receive wide support in the Commons, for every indication has already been given that there is no substantial opposition to such a measure. There should also be broad public support for this move.
Harrington Lodge, on Harrington lake, was acquired by the federal government several years ago as part of Gatineau park. To convert it to a summer home for the nation's prime ministers would require no large capital outlay ... It is only common sense to place the property at the Prime Minister's disposal . . . The country will benefit, because whoever is its prime minister can enjoy relaxation during the summer in a location virtually on Ottawa's outskirts.
Mr. Chairman, let me say in conclusion that we in the C.C.F. trust that the present and future prime ministers, including we hope future C.C.F. prime ministers, will find in this sylvan glade recreation, repose, rest and restoration of mind, body and spirit.

The object of this legislation, Mr. Chairman, is to ensure greater protection for labour as well as to provide for the stability of the unemployment insurance fund. The bill, of course, indicates to what extent this government thinks in terms of the have-nots; it follows upon the improvements introduced since the Conservative government came to power, and improves the unemployment insurance act in various ways.
The improvements brought about since June 1957 mean that $68 million have gone to the workers under various types of protection, when they were without jobs.
Mr. Chairman, the negative attitude of the Liberal opposition is inadmissible, since it is directly contrary to labour interests. All the noise made by our friends has but one purpose: to distract public attention so that people might forget about our friends' indifference towards labour.
The Liberals, as you know, in the course of the last two sessions, kept drumming into our ears: "What is the government going to do to help the unemployed whose unemployment insurance stamps are now exhausted?" Well, sir, we now have before us a bill designed to improve the situation. But, through their obstruction, Liberal members are merely delaying its adoption.

They objected so much that it has become impossible, Mr. Chairman, to adopt this bill for the 1st of July. As a result, the unemployed, that our Liberal friends want to hold so close to their heart as to stifle them-will be deprived, because of the lack of co-operation of the Liberals, of the aid that we, the Conservatives, wanted to give them.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the working people will not easily forget the lack of co-operation of those who criticize us for not doing enough for the working class.
Besides, because of their obstruction, according to the press, the delay in adopting Bill No. C-43 has deprived Canada of a great honour that was being done to it this year. In fact, according to the press, we know that our Minister of Labour had been asked to preside at the International Labour Congress which is to meet in Geneva. It is clear that our Liberals friends, who never had a similar honour offered to them, were quite disappointed about it. So, they went out of their way to force the minister to decline this invitation.
Mr. Chairman, I spent nearly twenty-five years of my life among workers, and I do not think I am boasting when I say that I know something about the sentiments of labour. Every weekend, so as to keep contact between grass and brass, I have interviews in my St. Hyacinthe office with workers of various classes and manufacturers of my city. I discussed this bill with them and all of them, without exception-whether they represent the textile or metal industry or any other industrial branch-recognize the necessity of this legislation and are unanimous in their support. The workers are pleased with the concern shown them by the Minister of Labour who can claim to have been a real workman himself. Therefore they are ready to play their part, knowing that if they do not personally benefit from the bill, some fellow-worker will. In referring to this matter at all, Mr. Chairman, I was trying to point out that we have maintained-and I think it was certainly maintained by the minister himself when he tabled one of the minutes of the advisory committee-that they have a bearing on the matter under discussion. I should just like to read from the submission made to the committee by the Canadian Manufacturers Association in which they point out the functions of the unemployment insurance advisory committee. They state as follows:
What was Intended to be and might well have been the most effective safeguard for the unemployment insurance fund is the unemployment insurance advisory committee. The act provides that it shall consist of a chairman and from six to eight other members. At least one of the members other than the chairman is to be appointed after consultation with organizations representative of employees and an equal number after consultation with organizations representative of employers.
The main function of the advisory committee under the act is to make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the unemployment insurance fund at the end of each fiscal year and at such other times as it thinks fit. If the fund is or is likely to be insufficient to discharge its liabilities or is more than reasonably sufficient to do so, the advisory committee is required to recommend appropriate amendments of the act or the regulations (Sec. 89). The governor in council may also direct the advisory committee to investigate (1) the provision of unemployment insurance for any excepted employments either by extending to it the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, modified if necessary, or by special or supplementary schemes: and (2) the rates of contribution and benefit of insured persons having regard to their earnings (Sec. 91).
The constitution of the advisory committee is based on the recommendations of the final report of the Gregory royal commission on unemployment insurance in England which in 1932 inquired into the provisions and working of the British unemployment insurance scheme.
Unfortunately the government has not always asked or paid attention to the advice of the advisory committee on the many important financial and other problems which have arisen during the eighteen years which the Unemployment Insurance Act has been in operation.
Because of the importance that has been attached to the advisory committee it was felt that this committee's findings and its deliberations were going to be heard by the committee. I think this procedure would only be fair if people were really interested in knowing what the situation was and what the situation was with regard to the recommendations of people appointed by various organizations to help decide on what amendments were necessary because of the unsatisfactory condition of the fund. I think that is only a fair assumption.
But if the government believes that political implications would accrue from such an investigation, then I can well understand the attitude taken. Having knowledge of what

its deliberations were the government and the chairman of this committee may well have decided that it would be advantageous to prohibit the investigation or the interrogation of the members of the advisory committee. However, when investigating and hearing the presentation of the first organization, namely the Canadian Construction Association, it was extremely interesting and most informative to note that their representative Mr. Urquhart also informed the committee that he was a member of the advisory committee. In discussing this matter with him and what he as a member of the advisory committee thought of the various amendments being proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act, I think many facts were obtained by the small amount of discussion that took place before this matter was ruled out of order.
It was at that time pointed out that you could not sit on these two organizations, and I was given to understand we would be able to call him at some later date when he could represent not the Canadian Construction Association but the advisory committee which he sat on. I think it is not fair for the chairman to say he could not represent two organizations, because he was appointed to that advisory committee by the government as a representative of this other organization. They just did not go out onto the street and pick up John Doe and say, "You are a member of the advisory committee". They chose him because he was a representative of this large body, the Canadian Construction Association.
So I think the committee was not given all the facts. They were not given an opportunity to discuss with these people who have a working knowledge of what was to be accomplished by the unemployment insurance fund what advantageous amendments might be made, and what the extent of the contributions must be to maintain the fund. They could have suggested, as he suggested every time he had the opportunity, that there were other fields of unemployment insurance besides those which were covered or expected to be covered under an actuarial basis. I think we would have found out that our contention made a few weeks ago when this bill was introduced at the resolution stage, because of the fluctuation and the boom and bust in unemployment and employment, was correct and that it was absolutely necessary to establish now two separate funds rather than trying to fit everybody into the unemployment insurance fund.
It has been pointed out that this fund had reached the sum of $900 million. When we asked this representative who had sat on the advisory committee if he felt that this was too high, he said that in his opinion
Unemployment Insurance Act he thought it was a suitable figure. He went on to point out, as did very one of the delegations which came before the committee in my attendance, that the fund now a little over $400 million was in an unsatisfactory position financially. Everyone, with no exception, pointed out they were opposed, and violently opposed, to the amendments now being introduced to the method of obtaining an increase in that fund by the contribution ratio of 40 per cent from the employees, 40 per cent from the employers and 20 per cent from the federal government treasury. In every case they suggested the contributions have to be rebalanced so that a bigger share of the contribution would come from the federal government treasury itself.
In the previous suggestion that two funds be set up, I think from the discussions that took place in the committee this is the only type of recommendation that the industrial relations committee should have brought in, that there has to be established from actuarial figures how many people are employed in a normal period of economy. It has been suggested that the unemployment in the years 1954-55 and 1957-58 was abnormal, and that even balanced out over a period of five years we would have to have sizeable increases in this fund which has now dropped from a figure of close to $900 million to a figure of $454 million. These figures do not take into consideration the unemployment in the period 1958-59. I think it is plain to all hon. gentlemen that if we are going to compensate for large scale unemployment which is not in an insurable category, then we are going to have a different type of fund, a fund which is to be taken out of general revenues and would put into circulation the amount of money we are not able to carry. If this fund, with the unemployment which has taken place in the two periods 1954-55 and 1957-58, excluding 1958-59, has been reduced by one-half, then I suggest we would not be able to carry the fund no matter what the contributions were increased to over the next two or three years, if the fund continued to be depleted at the rate it now is.
It has been suggested that these contributions, the 30 per cent we are being asked to grant, are going to produce something like $78 million. There has been a great deal of discussion, Mr. Chairman, as to whether that is the right figure or not. We have heard many discussions about what are the actual figures. The director of insurance has pointed out on several occasions that these figures are estimates. Apparently if you estimate it one way you get one set of figures, and if you estimate it in some other way you get a completely different set.	1

Mr. Humphrys, the assistant superintendent of insurance, stated that instead of the 78 per cent figure given to the house previously the amount of increased contributions would amount to $97 million. He also pointed out that rather than the $20 million that was going to accrue to the workers in benefits, it could be as high as $24 million. He pointed out that the benefit in extending the period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks was only going to cost $11 million. Those new categories would receive an estimated benefit of $9,400,000, and those in the higher earning categories would receive a benefit of $3,100,000. It has been pointed out by all the organizations that it is unfair to ask the people who are employed in steady employment, the people who are not going to be unemployed, the people who will in most cases not receive any benefits at all from this measure, to raise their contributions to pay the extra 30 per cent to raise a total of $97 million. This is not fair when the workers can at the maximum only receive in return a sum of $20 million or $24 million.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that this matter be returned to the committee and that the committee be empowered to investigate the reports-yes, and the resignations-of the advisory committee, and that we should go very carefully into their recommendations and find out at least why they were unanimously opposed to the decision that the government has now taken in moving amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

In a matter of this kind, following the prolonged discussion we had in this house on this bill and the discussion which took place in the committee, one would have thought, particularly in the light of the almost unanimous representations made by national employers' and employees' organizations in Canada, that the Minister of Labour would have taken advantage at the earliest opportunity to put forward the government's point of view on this very important proposal, which imposes a burden of almost $80 million a year more on the workers of this country and on the employer groups.
However, the minister is responsible for his own policy. He is responsible for his own actions, and I have no alternative but to indicate that thus far the only speaker from the government side who has addressed himself to this matter was the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot who said it was welcomed by the labour groups of this country, although, of course, such was not the case as has already been amply demonstrated, and as I will join my colleagues in proving.
We discuss this amendment now against a background of representations which have

been made by a number of national organizations representing both the employers and the workers of this country, all of whom, in a remarkable display of unanimity, expressed their keen dissatisfaction with this particular bill, a bill which has received at the hands of the opposition both before and during the discussions in committee, and now, in these proceedings, an expression of objection consistent with what we believe to be the merits of our case and of the representations made by these various national organizations.
We now have further information which was denied to us during the course of the debate on second reading, information which was made available to us by officials of the unemployment insurance commission, in particular, during the committee proceedings. We now know that the proposed additional contributions now run, on the average, not as we thought up to 30 per cent more, but from 25 to 56 per cent more, and this without any change in the pattern of benefits. We now know that while an additional $100 million by way of revenue will be derived from the additional contributions by the workers and employers and by the additional contribution of the government of Canada, there will be less than $25 million by way of benefit. We also know some of the reasons why the government, faced with the perilous state of the unemployment insurance fund, was obliged to come before parliament this year and recommend some particular method by which this perilous state of the fund-this trust fund, as it was referred to by the governor of the Bank of Canada-could be replenished, keeping in mind possible unemployment in the fall of 1959 and the winter of 1960.
We now know that the losses suffered by this trust fund practically equal the additional contributions which this measure seeks to impose on the two main groups of contributors, the workers and the employers of Canada. We know that there was an actual loss of over $10 million-a realized loss-as a result of the investment by the investment committee of some of the securities held by the unemployment insurance fund. We do know from the evidence which we were able to adduce from the governor of the Bank of Canada that there was, and that there is, a book loss at market valuation as of about a week ago of $62 million, which makes, at the moment, both in terms of a realized and an unrealized loss, a loss of $72 million. Undoubtedly that, together with the heavy drain on the fund as a result of serious unemployment-a problem which this government was going to correct-has placed the government in the difficult position, in the light of its future obligations, of seeking to replenish a

fund contributed to by the three main partners in Canadian society, a fund which at one time stood at over $800 million and which, when we began our deliberations, was revealed as having a book value in terms of its securities of about $496 million. But, as the hon. member for Welland pointed out last night, that fund at the present time, taking into account book values and taking into account what its securities will realize, stands at well below $400 million and closer to $350 million.
When one takes into account the amount of money which was required this year to provide maintenance for unemployed people who could qualify for benefit, it is clear that if we have comparable unemployment next fall and next winter there will not be sufficient money in the insurance fund to provide what these contractual arrangements, dedicated by an act of parliament, were intended to provide for the unemployed, for the workers of this country who made provision, along with the employers and the government and the people of Canada, for this measure of insurance in preparation for such a high level of unemployment as we have experienced during the past 18 months.
That is the situation. Hon. gentlemen opposite say we are holding up a bill which would bring great benefits to the workers of this country. Assuming, just for the sake of argument, that there was validity in that proposition, let it not be forgotten that this bill was referred to in the address from the throne last January. Let it not be forgotten that on this side of the house on four different occasions we urged the government to introduce this legislation in the early stages of this session. Let it not be forgotten that this bill was reported out of the committee on the ninth day of June, and we were told in the committee by the director of the unemployment insurance offices that in order to make its benefits applicable by June 28 the bill would have to be passed and considered in parliament by June 11.
What reason did the government have, assuming the validity of its arguments, which I deny, for not bringing this measure forward at once when the bill was reported? Why did not the government bring in this bill in the month of January, or in February? The reason, I suggest to you strongly, Mr. Chairman, is that notwithstanding all the advertisement in the speech from the throne, the government had not settled on a policy at all. That was the reason for these delays and now in the dying days of this session, in the face of the opposition which exists all over the country to this measure, hon. gentlemen opposite suggest that we have been holding up the legislation which they pretend
Unemployment Insurance Act will be of great value to the workers and the employers of this country, although it is a bill which does not change the pattern of benefit at all, a bill which provides benefits of less than $25 million and which exacts further impositions from the workers and employers of this country to an extent of almost $80 million. The hon. member for Welland was correct. What this government has done, faced with this serious situation, is to saddle on the workers of Canada and on the employers the responsibility of doing something which this government itself has failed to do. That is the real proposition that confronts us now as we begin in this chamber the discussion of this bill.
In this committee we were supposed to be given an opportunity of knowing all of the facts involved in this matter. "When we get to the committee," we were told by the minister "you will be able to inquire about this and about that." We went to the committee. I want to indicate how inconsistent were some of the positions of the majority of the members of that committee who made it impossible for the small minority represented by this group and the group sitting immediately to the left of Mr. Chairman to carry on their work and to ascertain what were the facts.
We had asked that the members of the unemployment insurance advisory committee, the men who by experience, representing labour and representing the employers, would have been in a position to tell us why they were opposed unanimously in the summer of 1958 to this particular formula of increased benefits unless the government contribution was made to represent one-half of the total contributions of the workers and of the employers. Were we given an opportunity of examining the members of the advisory committee? No. On two distinct occasions we tried pursuant to the suggestions made when we were debating this matter on second reading and pursuant to the reports that were tabled by the Minister of Labour-one of which was tabled with great reluctance by him-to arrange to interrogate the members of the advisory committee as to why they could not accept the formula proposed by way of additional contributions. No, that was something that had been denied the members of the House of Commons when this was discussed on second reading, it was alleged this allegation was contrary to the facts. No, this advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission had nothing to do with the bill and because of that no opportunity would be afforded to the members of this committee to ascertain from five employers

Unemployment Insurance Act and from five labour men and the chairman of that commission why that particular body was opposed to increasing the contributions without changing the pattern of benefits.
And to show how inconsistent was that position taken by the majority of the committee, a motion was made by the hon. and respected member for Hamilton South that we be given an opportunity to examine the members of the investment committee, the governor of the Bank of Canada and his two colleagues, the deputy ministers of labour and finance. That motion supported by the opposition was, of course, carried. What difference in principle was there in allowing us to examine, as we were properly entitled to examine, the members of the investment committee and at the same time denying us the right to examine the members of the advisory committee?
This government and the majority of the members of the government party on that committee will undoubtedly pass this bill by sheer force of numbers but in so doing the record will be clear that they denied the minority of the committee the right to examine the members of the advisory committee who more than any other group were seized with the reasons which justified or failed to justify this additional imposition on the workers of our country. That no hon. gentleman in this chamber can deny and there is no escape from that situation now for hon. gentlemen who sit to Mr. Chairman's right.

The estimate of new benefits which may result from higher allowable earnings will amount to something between $2 million and $3.3 million. Therefore, the total additional benefits provided by this bill will vary from $21.9 million to $25.3 million.
Now, let us look at the added revenue that is going to be derived from this measure. What is the expected additional revenue resulting from the addition of two new classes of contributions? Something between $15 million and $17 million, we were told. What will be the additional revenue derived from the raising of the income ceiling from $4,800 to $5,460? The answer is somewhere between $2 and $3 million. What will be the additional revenue provided by the increase of between 25 per cent and 56 per cent in the level of contributions? It will be somewhere between $75 million and $80 million. The government's contribution will be roughly $16 million. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the total increase in contributions of about $100 million, of which the government will pay about $16 million, is the revenue position. The workers and industry will pay $85 million more annually and will receive a little more than $20 million in additional benefit. That is in general the reason, one of the main reasons, why the opposition groups, representing in this instance the employers and labouring groups in Canada, are vigorously opposed to shouldering on labour and industry the responsibility that belongs to the government of Canada.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to move the second reading of Bill No. S-23, respecting the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Prince Rupert. As sponsor of this bill, it is my privilege to provide information to this house and reasons why favourable consideration should be given to its passage. The area served by the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Prince Rupert comprises 135,000 square miles between the 53rd and 58th parallels of latitude and from the Pacific to the Alberta border in British Columbia, including the Queen Charlotte islands. The total population of the area is between 85,000 and 90,000. The catholic population of 12,500 includes about 4,000 Indians. There are seven schools with four more in the process of being built, together with 12 churches and 12 rectories. This compares with four churches, four rectories and one school at the time of incorporation in 1924. Most of the towns in the area have doubled their population in the last five years. This recent increase and the anticipated increases in population are the reasons for the removal of the restrictions on the value of real estate held by the corporation and the period during which it may be held.
As to subclause 3 of clause 4 of the act in its present form, several recent statutes incorporating religious or eleemosynary bodies contain no limitation on the value of the real property which may be held by such bodies. Moreover, in several recent instances private acts have contained provisions removing such limitations not only for the future, but retroactively. Provisions imposing a time limit on the holding of unused real estate, such as are contained in subsections 4 to 7 inclusive of section 4 of the act in its present form have been omitted in some recent incorporations of religious bodies, such as the act to incorporate Oblate Fathers of Assumption Province and Bill No. S-18 which received third reading in the Senate on April 23 last, an act to incorporate the Lutheran Church of Canada.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fisher for the second reading of Bill No. C-10, to amend the Canada Elections Act (voting at advance polls).

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) introduced a similar bill at the last session of parliament, and at that time I supported the bill. I think it is rather significant that this bill was under discussion last year on June 17, one year ago tomorrow. I have not discovered any reason during the past year for changing my opinion about the bill in principle. The proposal by the hon. member for Port Arthur is a sound one.
I believe that the provision for voting at advance polls must be enlarged. I have certainly no intention, Mr. Speaker, of repeating the speech I made last year in connection with a similar bill. At that time I did mention various cases where the narrow provision of the act as it now exists prevented people from voting at advance polls who should have voted. I pointed out the provision which limits the class of persons who may vote, and there is a restriction even within that class. I felt also at that time that the ninth and tenth days before polling date were actually too early to give the voters a proper picture and a proper opportunity to evaluate their candidates.

Canada Elections Act
In view of the discussion we had last year, I took very special note of the voting in the recent Ontario provincial election, particularly with regard to advance polls. We all know, I believe, that in Ontario the privilege of voting at advance polls is very much the same as proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur. In other words, any person who is otherwise qualified to vote, and who has reason to believe he will not be present in the riding on polling day has the right to apply for and receive a ballot at the advance polls. There is no class of persons specified and there is no limitation on the persons who may vote. If a voter has good reason for believing he will be absent, then he may vote. I also noted during the provincial election that there did not seem to be any great rush of voters to the advance polls; there did not seem to be any snarls. I must say that I, myself, took advantage of the opportunity of voting at the advance poll in my home town when it appeared that I would be absent in Ottawa. I was rather pleased to have the opportunity of seeing how the voting was carried out and how it would work out if we used the same provision in federal elections. I certainly was unable to see any objection to it.
There have been objections raised to enlarging the class of persons who may vote at advance polls. One such objection is that too many people would vote and that, in effect, we would have four polling dates instead of one. This seems to have been an objection raised by the electoral officials, and it is one which has been raised from time to time by other persons. We have a rule that there shall be one polling day in Canada, and the fear is that we might have more than one if a large number of persons were to vote at advance polls. Certainly the experience in the past has not indicated that would happen in federal elections. The experience in the last provincial election has not indicated there would be that large number of persons voting so that there would be, in any way, an infringement of the rule against more than one polling day. I observed that the D.R.O. and the poll clerk seemed to have plenty of time to handle the votes, and in fact could have handled a great many more without any difficulty. For these reasons, I feel that this objection would not be valid.
I have heard it stated that enlarging the advance poll provision might make an election more expensive. This may be true to a very slight extent. I would imagine more forms would have to be printed, and so forth, but I cannot see that such a provision would necessitate any additional polls being established. The present provision for advance poll and those who present themselves the 
advance poll staff could handle three, four or five times as many voters as they do. I cannot see that any great increase in expense would be required.
There has not yet been sufficient time to analyse the results of the advance polls in Ontario during the recent election. From what I have been able to learn from electoral officials and others, I would say that no great difficulty was experienced and a lot more people could have been handled if they had appeared.
In so far as the hours of voting are concerned, the present act requires that the polls shall be open from two o'clock in the afternoon until ten o'clock in the evening. I am prepared to agree that this provision is proper and that there is no reason for changing it. I think that many people who are going to be away on voting day are people who would work during the day and who would have to have the privilege of voting in the evening in order to take any advantage of advance poll arrangements.
I should like to discuss for a moment the actual days when the advance poll should be held. I have done a great deal of thinking about this matter since it was raised last year and also since it was raised recently in the committee on privileges and elections. There are really three possible days or three possible sets of days on which the advance poll could properly be held. As proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur, the poll would be held on Friday and Saturday, the tenth and the ninth days before polling day. I said last year-and I am still of the same opinion-that this is quite a long time before polling day on which to hold the advance poll. It has, however, the advantage of including Saturday; and I think Saturday is an important day on which to hold an advance poll. Those who will be away during the week on voting day will have the advantage of voting on Saturday and I think that is essential.
We could also have the advance poll held as at present, namely on the Thursday, Friday and Saturday immediately preceding the polling day on Monday. Last year when the matter was discussed I felt that these were preferable dates and I still think so. I think this is the case in view of the fact that the actual number of people who will vote should not increase too much merely because of enlarging the class of people who may vote.
There is the difficulty that the advance poll is very close to the polling date and that if any cross-checking of lists is to be done as between those who have voted at the advance poll and those who present themselves the

following Monday it certainly does not leave much time for checking lists from the time when the advance poll closes on Saturday night until the time when the regular poll opens on Monday.
There is a third possibility which I should like to put forward and which I think would be worthy of consideration, namely that the advance poll might be held on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, the seventh, sixth and fifth days before the polling date. This time would appear to be most suitable. It is in accordance with the practice in Ontario and it is a reasonable time before polling day. It allows three days in which lists may be cross-checked, if such cross-checking is required, and it still is not too close to the voting day. The only difficulty with regard to Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday is that there is no Saturday voting date and there may be a class of persons who cannot vote on the Monday because they are away working and who would still be away on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of the previous week. I think the actual voting day is a subject that could very well be considered in the committee on privileges and elections. But pending any such decision I would feel that the present date-that is, Thursday, Friday and Saturday before polling date-would be the most suitable one.
The privileges and elections committee is now discussing the whole situation with respect to the elections act. However, the committee is at the moment considering only those suggestions that have been made by the chief electoral officer, ft is rather interesting to note that the chief electoral officer has not recommended any changes in the advance polling arrangements. What is being discussed-and what he has proposed-is mainly a series of procedural changes brought about to tighten up the provisions of the act and to prevent certain fraudulent and improper practices that prevailed as a result of two certain elections in recent times. I believe these amendments are suitable and will be adopted.
However, owing to the late date on which the election act was referred to the committee, the whole consideration of the act has not been undertaken and probably it will not be undertaken at this session. I am hopeful that next year the privileges and elections committee will have the act referred to it in its entirety and that we shall have broader terms of reference so that the act can be studied and revised throughout in preparation for the next general election.
I would also hope that next year the committee would be set up earlier so that it can get at this most important amendment and
Canada Elections Act
take some time at it. One of the difficulties of this committee this year has been that we were late in starting. We have been competing with a large number of other committees for attendance and it has been most difficult to get down to a serious discussion of the broader terms of the elections act. I think there is no point in referring the present bill to a committee at this session, particularly the privileges and elections committee. I know it is the intention at the next session to consider advance polling arrangements along with various other substantive changes in the act. If the bill should come to a vote today I would vote in favour of it because with the principle of it I am entirely in agreement. However, I do not think that this is a case where any particular advantage would be gained by bringing the bill to a vote.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house this afternoon is one of those hardy perennials that appear on the order paper from year to year. It is inevitable, of course, that all hon. members should be interested in the subject matter of the bill, namely increasing the interest and the percentage of the electors participating in our regular federal elections. One of the problems of democratic government is, the tendency for a large percentage of the voting population to be lukewarm in their interest in the electoral process. In recent years from time to time we have had drawn to our attention the fact that a relatively small number of voters, as compared with the total possible, exercise their franchise. In the past two federal elections there has been an encouraging increase in that percentage; but as we get down to the lower levels of government, particularly to the level of local government, we find that there has been unfortunately a declining interest. I think the hon. member for Port Arthur who is responsible for sponsoring the present bill before us is to be congratulated, because it is an attempt to deal with a small segment of the general difficulties arising from the operation of our democratic process.
In addition to the solution proposed-and I will go into further details in regard to the suggestion of enlarging the opportunities for advance polling-there are other ways and means of increasing interest in the electoral process and encouraging our voting population to exercise their franchise. In some countries, for example, resort has been made to the system of compulsory voting. I am always interested to hear comments from the chief electoral office in regard to suggested reforms of this kind. Our chief electoral officer for Canada is a man of vast experience.

Canada Elections Act
As a matter of fact, the post has been in the one family for two generations. The present incumbent worked alongside his father in that post and acquired all the experience of his father in that position, and now he carries on on his own from that broad perspective. In the recent meetings of the committee on privileges and elections it is interesting to note-and the previous speaker referred to this fact-that the chief electoral officer, the one who understands thoroughly the operations of our election machinery, is rather lukewarm to major reforms even of the kind indicated in the bill before us. With reference to the suggestion of compulsory voting, of course the major objection is that it is contrary to the spirit of the free exercise of the right to ballot, the right to exercise the franchise.
We have had other suggestions from time to time from members who have been subjected to the electoral process on one occasion or another. There is a feeling abroad today that we would create a broader interest in our federal elections if we shortened the duration of time occupied by elections. The modern means of communication and the improvement in the mass media of publication make it possible to put the issues much more quickly and effectively before the electorate, with the result that a long, drawn-out election period seems to dull the enthusiasm rather than increase the interest of the voter. These are merely two additional methods that have been proposed from time to time to encourage greater interest in the electoral process and to help in some measure to overcome the apathy that is unfortunately all too common in the responsibilities of democratic citizenship.
Coming specifically to the subject matter of Bill No. C-10, the suggestion that the privileges of advanced polling be broadened is one of the reforms that I think most obviously occurs to the candidate who has had at least one election experience. It has been my privilege to have stood for election during four campaigns. I recall in the first campaign that one of the most distressing reactions I received from the electorate in my constituency were the urgent complaints on election day that they had been involuntarily disenfranchised because of the restricted advanced polling privileges. As a newcomer to the political field I immediately made my protest in the only form available at that time-letters to the chief electoral officer. I have been interested to note as I have gathered more experience in campaigning that one of the most frequent and common complaints presented to the chief electoral officer is this one of the restricted advanced polling privilege. But the more experience acquired

in the field, the more one becomes aware that it is not so easy of solution as first glance would indicate.
I think the most glaring recent experience of the inequities of the restrictions occurred during the famous summer election of 1953, I believe it was, when the election occurred for the first time in many years on August 10. The date, of course, came at the peak of the Canadian holiday season and there was a great barrage of complaints from Canadians who were absent from their constituencies and were unable to cast their ballot. An interesting group in this class were teachers, who usually take a most active part in our democratic process. They found themselves studying at various universities across the country, taking summer courses to improve their qualifications in the teaching profession, and they were most incensed to discover that they could not exercise their franchise during that important election. At that time, being intelligent citizens keenly aware of public issues, they got together and made a concerted protest over the problem that this bill attempts to deal with. I imagine that subsequent to that occasion there was more discussion on this point in the House of Commons than we have had in a good many years.
I think the sponsor of this bill has laid this fact down as the main reason for the reform, and that is the increased mobility of our population under modern conditions of living. It is not uncommon to find segments of the Canadian population hundreds of miles away from the various constituencies during election period. This arises from the improved means of transportation as well, of course, as from the great expanse of geography in Canada.
While there is a solid case for a reform of this kind, and most hon. members who have spoken in the debate have generally expressed their support for the principle, there are some real technical problems arising from changes in the operation of the electoral machinery which have caused the chief electoral officer, the authority on these matters, to have rather a negative opinion as to its effectiveness. The problem of setting up a sufficient number of advance polls to cater adequately for voters in our larger constituency areas is one that must cause serious second thoughts. The privilege of voting at advance polls would, of course, have to be extended universally, if at all, and some of the areas involved cover hundreds of miles. The provision of adequate advance poll facilities would obviously mean a considerable financial outlay. In my own constituency, which is an average western prairie constituency, we have two advance polls only, and even in present circumstances

the distances involved are great enough to disenfranchise some of those who would otherwise be interested in casting their ballots.
Then, too, we must consider another difficulty, namely that all the issues would, probably, not be presented to the voters before the day of the election. In my experience in four election campaigns I found that very often the last two days before the election were the crucial days. The most successful campaigns are those which begin slowly and build up to a climax on the eve of the election. Sometimes basic issues are withheld until the final days, or even hours of the campaign for the specific purpose of stimulating interest in the election and reaching the climax of the campaign just at the precise psychological moment. These are all matters which have to be taken into consideration when we are contemplating making amendments to the Canada Elections Act as purposed in Bill No. C-10.
Returning to my original theme, I take it that the sponsor of this measure has as his main purpose in proposing the amendment a desire to increase the turn-out of the electorate at the polls, a desire to make it possible for every Canadian to exercise his franchise. If that were the basic motivation behind this amendment, the present bill would, of course, have only a relatively small impact on this problem, because even with extended advance poll facilities there would still be a large number of voters in Canada who would not be able to exercise their right to vote. That situation arises mainly because of increased mobility. The present arrangements restrict advance poll privileges to a relatively short period of time. As has been said by the former speaker, it might be desirable, if the house contemplates proceeding with amendments of this kind, to change the present days prior to the election in which it is possible to vote at an advance poll-to advance it by several days. Even this, of course, would exclude some people who might be absent from their constituencies at that particular time.
One way of approaching this problem might lie in extending absentee voting privileges. All members of the armed forces who served overseas during the second world war will recall that absentee voting was carried out efficiently in all parts of the world. For example, I remember casting my ballot in the city of Cairo in the election of 1945 which, I believe, took place in June of that year, and I had no difficulty at all in obtaining information concerning the candidates and their qualifications. The principle of absentee voting has been established in connection with
Canada Elections Act
the armed forces and if the technical difficulties were overcome its more general adoption would increase to a substantial extent the ability of Canadians to participate in elections no matter where they were on election day.
This matter, together with the general subject of amendments to polling privileges, has been under discussion in the committee on privileges and elections. The previous speaker indicated that this committee, of which I happen to be a member, got under way at rather a late date in the parliamentary session, with the result that we will not be able to come to grips with some of the complexities of this subject. However, there is still ample time before another election to investigate thoroughly these proposals. It is my wish and hope that during the next parliamentary session considerable time will be taken in examining the proposals of the chief electoral officer in this regard and in examining the implications of amendments such as this which we have before the house this afternoon. I say this because I think it is vitally important that this house should make it possible, as far as we are physically able within the restrictions of the electoral machinery, for every Canadian who desires to do so to cast his ballot.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a very wise practice to review and, if necessary, amend the Canada Elections Act every ten years, otherwise we shall probably be stuck with a lot of outdated rules and regulations which would not coincide with the changes in the manner in which we are trying to live. At the present time I understand the committee on privileges and elections is holding meetings, and although this year the committee started a little late I have no doubt that when the report comes in it will contain several proposals, some of which will possibly have to do with advance polls.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) when he was explaining the bill and my reaction to this proposed legislation is somewhat along the following lines. If the privilege of voting at an advanced poll were extended to include all the people who are entitled to vote instead of just to restricted classes as at present such as commercial travellers, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, fishermen and others, we would require a greatly increased number of advance polls.
If I may become personal for a moment I should like to refer to my own constituency of St. Antoine-Westmount where we had one advance poll in the last two federal elections. If the privilege of voting at advance

Canada Elections Act
polls were extended to all eligible voters the number of polls required in each constituency would vary. Approximately ten advance polls would be required in my constituency. I am doubtful however, that they would serve any great purpose. Approximately thirty votes were cast at the advance poll in my riding in the last two elections. It seems to me that the extension of this privilege would result only in increased expenditures for the crown without serving any great need. It is true that my constituency is urban and it may be that rural ridings would require a different set-up to take care of the matter.
Another consideration is that if this proposed bill were to become law, instead of a general election lasting one day it would last perhaps three days. Most of us are nervous enough having to sustain a one-day election and I do not know how we could suffer through an election lasting three or four days.
My understanding of the act as it now stands is that it requires a returning officer to notify the deputy returning officer as to the number of people who have voted at the various polls. The extension of the privilege proposed by this bill would put a considerably increased load on the shoulders of the returning officers in ensuring that all the deputy returning officers have been notified and that there are no cases of fraud, intentional or not.
I understand that advance polls exist in Ontario for the benefit of any voter and that in introducing this innovation the number of advance polls had to be increased from approximately 240 to approximately 1,100. This was an expensive propositon. As the result of the increase in advance polls the province of Ontario managed to merely double the number of voters from approximately 5,000 to approximately 10,000. This would appear to be an indication that the public is not much interested in having this privilege. The people who do not want to vote are not going to vote in any event and I do not know that we are right in worrying too much about them. I might say that the figures I used for the purposes of this illustration were taken not from the election held on June 11 last but from the previous one. The figures concerning the June 11 election are not available as yet.
I would suggest that instead of advance polls it would be much better if it were possible to establish a permanent election list so that everyone could have, as it were, a voting credit card or something of that nature and thus a voter from Halifax could vote in Vancouver at an advance poll. It is true that if this suggestion were implemented

it would cost in the neighbourhood of $4 million or $5 million to maintain the list up to date, but it is perhaps deserving of consideration. One disadvantage I can readily see is that there would be a delay in obtaining election results. One would have to wait for ten days or two weeks before the full results came through. The armed services have an absentee voting arrangement but they begin voting three weeks before the general public and despite that early start there is a delay of a week or more in tabulating and returning the results.
I suppose it is trite to say that the privilege of voting is one given to all citizens of Canada who have reached age 21 and that we should not stand in the way of anyone exercising his right to vote no matter what it cost the country but I think we sometimes are inclined to go a little too far in the direction of allowing people to take advantage of statutory provisions that are laid down and perhaps we should encourage them to take the initiative with respect to the basic freedoms.
As I say, approximately 30 votes were cast at the one advance poll in my riding in the last two elections and on the basis of my observations I fail to see how the proposed bill would serve to increase the number of votes cast to any valid degree in proportion to the total cost not only in dollars but in the expenditure of man-hours and energy. It was suggested by some previous speakers that the advance polls be opened a week or ten days in advance. This would give you less time in which to conduct your election. There is already talk of attempting to shorten elections but if the time were reduced to five or six days it would not give a candidate very much time in which to place his views before the people.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to state my position with regard to the matter raised by consideration of bill C-10 now before the house. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I regret that, because of the limited time at my disposal, I shall not be able to go into any details.
However, I want to tell this house that the franchise is obviously a sacred right, one on which our whole democratic system rests, and any legislation designed to promote the exercise of that right should obviously be encouraged by those very people who represent the nation. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, you will realize that, if we have the franchise, we should also consider it our responsibility to avail ourselves of this right, and that the exercise of a duty necessarily implies some degree of personal sacrifice.

Bill C-10 tends to promote the use of the right to vote, but there are, nevertheless, car-tain technicalities to observe when carrying out such duty. Therefore, I wonder how we can go about establishing a large number of advance polls throughout the country unless certain restrictions are imposed in respect of the exercise of franchise. Obviously a privilege is always granted for very special reasons or in extraordinary circumstances.
For instance, there are advance polls for commercial travellers, for seafarers, for fishermen or railway employees. Those people's life-work force them to be away from their home for long periods of the year. It is therefore reasonable that the law should grant them some special privilege in the exercise of their franchise. However, as far as the citizens of this country in general are concerned, I think we should think twice before passing a bill like the one introduced this afternoon.
In brief, this legislation provides that for some reason or other, a citizen should have the privilege of voting in an advance poll.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I think that if we approve such a bill, without further specifying the reason which a voter who wants to avail himself of his franchise might put forward, we might run into complications that might be very hard to get around, and, in addition, as mentioned by the previous speaker, because many rural ridings in Canada are so large, the establishment of advance polls would give rise to a good number of technical difficulties and also mean a tremendous expense.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the committee responsible for studying part of the Canada elections act should continue its research work so as to determine more clearly the elements of this bill while not losing sight of the fact that we should encourage Canadian citizens, whatever their country of origin, to use their franchise and thus actually share in their country's government. Moreover, those technicalities should be clearly set out and the privilege only be granted for very special reasons and in extraordinary circumstances which, I think, should be defined in the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am in general agreement with the intent of this bill. I
Canada Elections Act
have spoken on this matter in the house before. I have in my election campaigns found people who were deprived of their franchise through no fault of their own. They had to go to hospital. In one case I know of, an auditor was accompanying his salesman. If he had had a letter saying that he was a salesman he could have voted, but he could not; he was an auditor. Therefore, he did not vote but the salesman did.
As far as the expense referred to by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Webster) is concerned, I checked in my own riding on the advance poll which was open for two days between the hours of two and ten p.m., and there was hardly anybody coming in. The total advance poll would have been about 150 and they could easily have taken care of eight times that number. Therefore, although there might necessarily be more advance polls set up in a riding, I do not think it would be of the order of the magnitude that the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount indicated.
I do agree with the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) when he said that expense is not the criterion in regard to whether a person should have the right to exercise his franchise or not. Parliament is an expensive institution. In many ways it is an inefficient institution; but the people of Canada and the people of the western world are willing to pay the monetary price to have parliament because through parliament they have democratic government. Therefore, it is not a question of how much it will cost but it is a question as to whether we are depriving any citizen of a right which is his and which any government should be most anxious to maintain and to make it possible for that citizen to exercise that right if he wishes to do so.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Musko-ka (Mr. Aiken) did point out that the time- and this is one place where I find myself in disagreement with the bill-at which the advance polls are held is on the tenth and ninth days before the regular polling day. I assume that is because in many ridings the returning officer has to send the lists to the deputy returning officers, and give time for those lists of people who have used the advance poll to get into the hands of the deputy returning officers. It does seem to be an excessive length of time.

I suggest to the hon. member for Essex East that a good part of the membership of this advisory committee had resigned.
