What the hon. member for Essex East wanted was the minutes. What hon. members opposite really wanted was the minutes of the unemployment insurance advisory committee, a privileged document. Moreover, there would have been found in those minutes no information that was not in the report that was tabled a long time ago.
Then we have another strawman, another smokescreen and this one really caught fire. Do you know what it was, Mr. Chairman? I will tell you. Here is what it was. The hon. member for Essex East tried to give the impression that we were really overburdening the employers and the employees of this nation. Oh, this was a terrible thing, according to him. Why? I will tell you why, Mr. Chairman. Hon. members opposite, in past years during the Liberal administration, when things really became tough with the unemployment insurance fund, said that they came to the rescue of it by whopping big transfers from consolidated revenues. I thought that might have been a good point so on my own behalf I did a little bit of investigating and do you know what I found? Do you know what these whopping big transfers were? In a fund that sometimes reached practically $1 billion, the whopping big transfers amounted to $1,800,000. That is the way in which they came to the rescue of the workers of this country. Let us keep the record straight and things in proper proportion.
Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, appeared before this committee. By hon. members opposite he was subjected to exactly the same treatment as that accorded to other witnesses: no questions. Here we had one of the senior civil servants of this country appearing before a committee in order to help us make legislation for the
[Mr. Grafftey.l
benefit of the workers of this country and what did we have? We had one political statement after another from hon. members opposite. Up went the strawman; up went the smoke. It all caught on fire and chaos reigned. Then they have the temerity to tell us that the chairman allowed things to get out of order. The hon. member for Essex East was wily but I suggest that there are two sides to every story. I hope I am exposing the other side now.
They talked about losses in the unemployment insurance fund. I suggest that they talked about losses before they were ever realized and that they arrived at the calculation of these losses, even in the face of the expert testimony given by Mr. Coyne of the Bank of Canada, without taking into account any interest gained from the bonds. I suggest that that is another side of the coin which they might have looked at.
In analysing the position of Mr. Coyne on this investment committee hon. members opposite tried to point out that his position was incompatible. I think it was an interesting argument and I am going to try to discuss it in as cool and objective a way as possible. They tried to point out to the committee that his position on the investment committee of the unemployment insurance fund was incompatible with his job as a senior adviser to the Minister of Finance. I should like to point this out to you, Mr. Chairman. Time and time again Mr. Coyne told the committee that a fund of this nature could not be considered outside the principles of sound national debt management.
But I was not surprised because this is not the first time that hon. members opposite have tried to divide labour's interest from the national interest. I well remember sitting in that committee when one of the hon. members opposite said this, "Mr. Chairman, we have heard the brief of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. Tomorrow we shall hear the other extreme, the other side of the story". I say that the attitude here is wrong. Hon. members opposite went into that committee and tried to show the people of Canada that they were the champions of labour and that we, by this legislation in particular and by our attitude in general, were against labour. Such is not the case, Mr. Chairman. That is part of their game of divide and rule. As everyone well knows, this government has created a marvellous atmosphere of co-operation between management and labour and in turn between management, labour and government. In the future I should like all members of this house to refrain from trying to use measures of this type for political purposes and for political gain. I would have

thought that bipartisanship should have been underlined in touching upon measures of this nature.
Mr. Chairman, remark after remark was made in the committee, as it has already been made in the house during the debate, to the effect that since this party came to power the fund has gone into a terrible decline. The first question I put to hon. members opposite is this. Would they suggest that the government should have withheld payments from the unemployed men in Canada during the recent recession? I ask that question because, let us be frank, forthright and sincere, that is the major and only reason why there was a drain on the fund. But we were told that since we came to power there has been a terrible decline in the fund. We were told this in spite of the expert testimony we were given by officials of the Department of Labour, who told us in their report that the per capita value of this fund started declining back in 1953 and 1954. Another straw man burned.
I think it is obvious why this legislation has been brought forward. I am not going to get caught up in what I call a philosophical argument as to whether it is a welfare or an insurance fund. I put the question on repeated occasions to witnesses who appeared before the committee, and even they were not clear in their thinking. No more do I feel should I get into a debate at this point as to what constitutes putting the fund on a sound actuarial basis. Admittedly many of the briefs brought before the committee, which I think treated the matter logically, did suggest that those parts of the fund which smacked of welfare notions perhaps should be handled under a separate management; and the Minister of Labour repeatedly replied to hon. members on the committee that this question was being given careful, active and fast consideration by his department. I would suggest that especially when the government pays the administrative costs of this fund it will be difficult to determine when, how and if you can put it on a sound actuarial basis. This is only a personal observation, but it is more than an insurance fund; it is an insurance-welfare fund, and I think we should be realistic and regard it as such.
I would like to say it is my view that, if the committee was not subjected to such a long filibuster this legislation would have been passed long ago ;find the workers of this country would long ago have been able to take benefit of the 52 week period. But such is not the Case. I suggest we saw in that committee one of the all-time great political filibusters, and I think it is about time the workers of this country knew. Unemployment Insurance Act

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in the debate on this bill. However, after listening to certain speeches by hon. gentlemen opposite, I thought it my duty to rise and state my views. I represent the riding of Lafontaine, which has a sizeable labour population in addition to people in other walks of life and I think I ought to say a few words tonight on this bill.
After I had read and re-read this bill, I heard the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) tell us that the working class, who are excellent people, recognized this legislation to be in their own best interests.
It is true that I do not represent the people of St. Hyacinthe nor, in particular, the working class of that riding. But I am speaking on behalf of the workers in my own riding.
I am the member for Lafontaine, but I have to represent in this house all the people in this country. When I sit here in the Commons, I am conscious of my responsibility. I know that when some issue arises in parliament, I have to face it as it is, with all its consequences. Therefore, when I cast my vote, I do so in all sincerity, in the best interest of the people of Lafontaine riding, as well as of all parts of Canada. Indeed, it is impossible to represent just one riding, even if we should attempt to safeguard the interests of the people who sent us here. The bill which has been submitted to this house must be considered on its merit with regard to the people of each province, and even more so when it does not favour the whole Canadian working class.
After listening to the hon. member. I feel I am in a position to tell him that he is ignoring the facts when he says that we wanted to delay the adoption of this bill. Besides, I disagree with him all the more because the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe knows perfectly well that the social measures introduced here in the house to help labour, such as the Unemployment Insurance Act, were indeed introduced by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King.
You will probably say that, after the measure became law, amendments were made as needed to meet certain cases which could occur. But, when it is suggested that the Liberal members on this side of the house are delaying the adoption of a law which
[Mr. Grafttey.l
provides for the welfare of the population, I say: "No! you can't get away with that" because only the Liberal party, my hon. friend, from St. Hyacinthe, can introduce legislation to help labour. Furthermore, I challenge you to name one which has not been introduced for that purpose. So, now that you are part of the government, go ahead and introduce logical measures in the interest of the population and we will support them.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Don't venture too far in that direction, because we might have something to say too.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was wrong to suggest any such thing. Moreover, what had been done for labour was being ignored when the members on the committee were refused all the required opportunity to gather the information necessary for a detailed study of the bill. Really, I could not make head or tail of the reasoning of the member for St. Hyacinthe when he tried to explain what happened when he was sitting on the committee.
Mr. Chairman, what is going on here at present seems to me very strange, especially since the Conservative party has been sitting on the other side of the house, not so much from a political standpoint as from a legislative standpoint.
When the Conservatives were on this side of the house, everything was allowed, and now that they are on the other side, nothing is allowed. But, good heavens, why doesn't the government accept our opinion when we have something significant to offer, as we used to do when we were on the other side? Isn't that so, Mr. Chairman? You were here and you know that under the Liberal administration, when the opposition suggested an amendment calculated to improve a bill, we accepted it. We did not act in a narrow partisan spirit, like the government members do now.
It is time to put a stop to this policy of strife because it is not in the public interest. The public needs protection, and if you do not protect the electors, tomorrow the electors will not protect you. It is time to put a stop to those fights that are not in the interest of the population.
I was telling you a while ago that I was astonished. Listening to the speech made by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe this evening, I remembered the speech made on March 27, 1957 by the present Minister of

Finance (Mr. Fleming) during the budget debate for the fiscal year 1957-58 where-I only took a few notes,-as reported on page 2557 of Hansard for March 21, 1957, he criticized his predecessor. The then minister of finance, Mr. Harris, had predicted in 1956-57 a surplus of $112 million which at the end of the fiscal year increased to $382 million. However, taking into consideration the budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance and on the basis of the same expectations we are justified in believing that he will end the 1958-59 fiscal year with a $422 million deficit. If we had so much money, how is it that the deficit should be so high now and that we should be showing such heavy losses?
Mr. Chairman, if there was so much money in the fund and if, in spite of that we have become so poor, it is because unemployment has increased. However, I regret to say this, but that has not happened under a Liberal government and the Conservatives are responsible for it. I know what I am talking about because I have noticed that in my constituency and in the neighbourhood, an industry which had 6,000 employees on its payroll in March 1957, had only half as many by September of the same year. In another industry where there were 6,800 employees, there were only 2,000 a few months later. That has happened because those industries lost contracts they had held, and consequently, work had stopped. Therefore, it is time to react.
I must add that if the unemployment insurance fund is absolutely in need of aid- as I have already indicated during the debate on the speech from the throne, last year- the government must take care of it. I think the existing deficit should not be hidden, and should not be made up by contributions extracted from the employee and the employer. It should be divulged so that we may realize the full extent of the deficit of the unemployment insurance fund, and of the financial difficulties that this country must face.
I will be brief, because I do not like long speeches. But I think it is a pity that, after so many years of prosperity, there should be so much hardship, so many people destitute looking for work and unable to earn a living. I believe that we should draw the required money from the consolidated revenue fund, and not from the employer's and employee's pockets.
The time has come to put an end to it. That is my last word.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear! Hear!

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
But in heaven's name, let us put an end to this fratricidal strife and let
Unemployment Insurance Act us get together in helping out the poor people! Let us try to draft sensible legislation, in the best interest of society. If we were living in contentment in 1956-57, why should the years 1958-59 be years of discontent? Let reasonable legislative measures be introduced and if you ever happen to make a mistake, be honest about it, and we shall help you. But do not carry on as you do now.
Even if I am alone to do so, I will not support this Bill C-48 unless some amendment is introduced in favour of the employer and of the employee. I am prepared to do my very best, provided the government is sincere. I am the workers' servant, I know unions and I know their needs. I have never been in favour of paying $12,000 to someone who earns only $10,000, or $110 to a man who earns only $1,000. I have always supported the workers' fair and reasonable claims and I have fought for those people at the city hall. I even fought my own party for the sake of the working population whom I represent. As a candidate, I did not come forward as a labour man, but as a representative of labour, aware of the responsibilities of his mandate.
That is all I have to say tonight. For the common good of the people, I would like to see an end to all this strife, so that we can all lead a happier life.

I can
assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not intend to take up much of the time of the committee this evening, because there has been so little argument put up by the opposition that I am sure the committee will be ready to put this measure through without delay.
However, in the industrial relations committee we did receive a number of briefs, and I think it is only fair that something should be said about those briefs in answer to some of the representations which were made.
One of the big cries of the opposition has been that we should increase the contributions and that they should come out of the consolidated revenue fund but no argument has been put forward to support why this should be done. Hon. members of the opposition merely keep on screaming and raving in this respect hoping to create the impression that in their suggestions they are favouring labour. I think this represents a dangerous suggestion and during the course of my remarks I shall attempt to make a comparison between our unemployment insurance fund and the unemployment insurance fund of the United States where no

Unemployment Insurance Act proper contribution is made to that fund by employees. I shall offer this comparison in an endeavour to illustrate some of the dangers that can arise when the fund is not properly financed and is not paid into to a proper extent by the people who are going to benefit from it.
I have gone over the annual reports for the past three years and taken from there figures showing the contributions that have been made to the fund in Canada. In doing so I have been eager to ensure that my figures would be better than those we have been accustomed to hearing from the Martin bureau of statistics and to this end I have checked my figures with an adding machine. The contribution of the government for the three years 1956, 1957 and 1958 amounted to $197 million in round figures. I shall ignore the small amounts and express the figures to the nearest million. The three-year cost for administration and seasonal benefit was $184 million. In actual fact, then, the government has paid for the administration of the act and for seasonal benefits.
One of the arguments advanced has been that seasonal benefits have been a drain on the fund. That is the reason advanced for the government increasing its contribution from consolidated revenue. Another argument put forward was that the advisory committee made the recommendation that the government should increase its contribution. I dealt with this matter in the committee but I should like to bring it to the attention of hon. gentlemen now.
While the advisory committee is an admirable board and is able to offer advice to the unemployment commission on many matters it must be remembered that the board is made up of four members representing management and four members representing labour. When the witnesses from the Canadian Labour Congress were present in the committee I made the following suggestion. I said that if there was going to be a suggestion made that the burden should be taken from the employees and placed on the general taxpayers of the country, would they not agree that some representatives of the general taxpayers should be present in order to have some say in the matter? I indicated that I felt it was rather beyond the scope of the advisory committee to make a suggestion of that nature. Mr. Jodoin said that that is what the members of parliament are here dor, to protect the interests of the general taxpayers. That is why I make the suggestion now that the fund has to be properly paid into by those who are going to benefit from it.
In the United States the government makes no contribution whatever to the.fund:i They

have a tax of 3 per cent on all payrolls in the United States. Of that tax 0.3 per cent is taken for the administration of the fund so they pay nothing into it. As a result the United States legislation is not nearly as effective as ours. There are many reasons for this. In the first place the Canadian Labour Congress suggested that the ratio of the benefit to wages is not sufficient and that it should be approximately 60 to 75 per cent. In the United States, because employees do not pay a proper share of the fund, it has steadily been reduced and at the present time the ratio is only 30 per cent compared with 50 per cent in Canada.
I wish now to refer to a booklet entitled, "Comparison of State Unemployment Insurance Laws as of August 1954", a publication of the United States department of labour on page 72 of which we find the following:
Ten states have more specific provisions for reducing benefits in one or more respects when the fund falls below a specified amount or a specified ratio to benefit payments for a given period. California's is the most general of these provisions: if the commission determines that the fund will be unable, within six months, to pay probable benefit liabilities in full, it may, by rule, reduce or cease such payments.
Drawing the information from the above publication, let me point out some of the other actions that may be taken by various state governments in the United States whenever they see fit. They may reduce the minimum weekly benefit, reduce the duration of benefit, increase the waiting period, change the qualifying requirements, eliminate part of the benefits and reduce dependants' allowances. That is the sort of thing that happens when a fund is not properly financed.
A leading spokesman for the Liberal party, the hon. member for Essex East, feels that many people under the act should be on some form of relief and should not be under the act at all. I believe he made that clear in his remarks this afternoon. I can see no reason for taking that attitude at the present time. The people that are included under the act in the present amendments are not going to be any detriment to the act. He could therefore have been referring only to those who have been covered by the act for some length of time. As I said in the committee I had rather hoped that the thought today would be that we wanted to give the Canadian people these benefits as a right and not have them given at the whim of a government which could change its mind or increase the benefits for election purposes and reduce them at another time. I am sure the people of this country do not want to go back to some1 system of relief which is the only alternative ,to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

This was their recommendation to the federal government:
Among the proposals for action by the federal government was the provision of a greatly expanded program of public works: the provision of funds to subsidize housing and thus permit N.H.A. interest rates to be lowered, and the introduction of a budget which would reduce taxes to provide increased purchasing power.
In addition, the government was urged to increase unemployment insurance benefits and lengthen benefit periods for unemployment insurance; increase the federal share of unemployment assistance from 50 per cent to at least 75 per cent; increase old age pensions, family allowances, and other social security payments; raise farm purchasing power, and adopt a generous program of aid to underdeveloped countries.
We are getting along pretty well with this program but it is going to take a little more time. I think the general membership would realize that if we are going to do all these things we are going to pay a little more money to get them. This is my opinion from the contacts I have had with the average working people in my riding. The maximum amount that is going to be paid under this proposed scheme is 94 cents a week by way of contributions from the employee. This is the amount that will be paid by anybody who is making over $70 a week. I am quite satisfied that every working man in this country is quite willing to pay that amount to protect himself and get 52 weeks benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
One of the other matters which came up in the committee was the one which the hon. member for Timiskaming raised this afternoon, namely that there should be two funds and that some people should be taken out of this fund. I do not know how he is going to describe a seasonal worker. He indicated in the committee that seasonal workers should not be in this fund, although I have already pointed out the government pays more money into this fund than is necessary to cover the seasonal benefit and the administration of the act.
I went out the other day to the offices of the unemployment insurance commission and looked very carefully over the result of the operation of the fund in the last few years. At the committee I asked repeatedly who was described as a seasonal worker and we got varying answers. Some said fishermen; some said loggers. What I would like to know is where anybody would draw the line. I started to go down the list and I found that construction was very close. It was third behind the loggers and the

It seems to me that if we started to follow that principle all down the line pretty soon we would be getting to the point where those who were working would not have to pay into the fund at all, and the end result would be that we would not have any Unemployment Insurance Act at all. That is the only conclusion one can come to. You are going to have to build up the fund. Obviously, there would be no sense in not having it because if we did not have it we would have to go back to some system of relief.
What I am pointing out is this. The opposition are presenting these arguments that the money should come from the consolidated revenue fund. They must know in their own minds that if the federal government started contributing to this fund as a welfare scheme it would not be very long until we would have people from one end of the country to the other demanding that there should be a means test. That is a thing the working people of this country do not want. They want to know that when they are out of work they are going to be protected as long as necessary. These representations were made to me in my own riding when I was home between sessions last year, that we should extend the benefits of the act.
I pointed out to the Canadian Labour Congress in Vancouver at that time that it was all very well to have this, because I was perfectly in favour of that, and I said, "We shall also have to increase the contributions". They see the dangerous elements that I have referred to in the United States where the rates of benefits are lowered, where they are not even guaranteed any payment and where at the whim of the state government the payments can be cut off tomorrow. I am sure the working people of this country will be very well satisfied with the amendments we are putting through here.

Mr. Chairman, there are some other aspects of this matter which, I believe, require discussion in this committee. It was indicated this afternoon that the unemployment insurance fund must be regarded, in every sense of the word, as a trust fund. We have had pointed out to us that when this government took office the unemployment insurance fund was over $800 million, and that at the present time, taking into account the securities in the unemployment insurance fund and their related market value, that fund is now under $400 million, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $350 million.
We are called upon to deal with a proposal for increasing the contributions made by three contributors, notably the employers and employees, largely because of the depleted Character of the fund. It is our duty and our responsibility to inquire why the fund has reached, to use the language of the advisory Committee, the perilous state in which it is

now to be found. Undoubtedly the main reason for the drain on the fund is the fact that during the past 18 months this country has experienced the highest level of unemployment since the days of 1930-35. While we are all happy in the thought that we did have a fund, created largely as a result of contributions by employers and employees, we all regret that circumstances, some of which were within the control of this government, have been such as to cause the fund to reach this present stage of dangerous depletion.
Not only is the fund in this dangerous state because of the heavy drain made on it during the past 18 months by a high level of unemployment but because, at the same time, there has been an obligation imposed on the government, and on parliament, to provide ways and means for the maintenance of unemployed workers and their families, unemployed workers who were no longer able to qualify for the normal unemployment insurance benefits. We sought in this parliament to give assistance to this group by seasonal benefits.
This practice, as the Minister of Labour pointed out earlier tonight when he interrogated me, had been established by the previous administration. However, the difference between the situation in that regard in relation to the fund under the previous administration and under the present government is that the former, on three distinct occasions when it did provide for assistance by way of what were called then supplementary benefits out of the fund, took occasion to replenish that fund out of consolidated revenue. This was done on three occasions. The Minister of Labour pointed out that this was done on the first occasion only in the amount of some one million and several hundred thousand dollars. That is true. But that situation arose because that was the extent of the replenishment that was then required. But as the Minister of Labour also knows, on the two subsequent occasions the amounts refunded to the fund were larger proportionately to the amounts paid out of the fund.

In the industrial relations committee we dealt with an extremely important aspect of this matter that has not been fully dealt with yet. The government comes to parliament and says that the fund is in a perilous state; the labour representatives and the employer representatives on the advisory committee have said that the fund had reached an extremely perilous position. The government now says we must replenish the fund because we may have unemployment on a serious scale next fall and next winter. We say that it is not fair, just or in keeping with the traditions of this legislation-which was introduced by a Liberal administration in the dark days of war-to impose on the two main contributing groups an obligation which, just as in the case of public assistance, must be widely shared. No hon. gentleman from the government benches who has spoken in this debate thus far has dealt with this point. What justification is there for imposing on these two particular groups the responsibility of providing assistance to men and women in this country who, having exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits, require assistance from the national community? Why should that burden be imposed upon those two groups? That is the main point of our opposition to this measure; and no one speaking on behalf of the government has yet addressed himself to this point.
Mr. Chairman, we contended on second reading of this bill-and it is the argument which we made in the committee and which we make now-that if there were mistakes in the way in which this particular unemployment insurance fund was handled with
Unemployment Insurance Act regard to its investments, the consequences of lack of judgment or incompatibility of function should not be laid on the shoulders of the two main contributing groups.
We were told by the governor of the Bank of Canada, an able and competent public official-as we would have been told, I am sure, by the deputy minister of finance and the spokesmen for the Department of Labour who share with the governor of the Bank the responsibility for the investment of the unemployment insurance fund-that in the exercise of their responsibilities they had sought to display, to demonstrate and to exercise the best possible judgment. I have no quarrel with their good intentions nor do I in any way suggest bad faith on the part of any one of these three gentlemen. But the fact of the matter is that with respect to this fund they had the responsibility-just in the same manner as any trustee of any fund has a responsibility toward the fund he administers-to make as their exclusive concern the problems of and all the circumstances attending the trust fund. Under any trustee act in the administration of any estate in the discharge of any responsibility as trustee there is imposed, both by way of the written and the unwritten law, an obligation on the part of the trustee to regard as his exclusive concern the interests and the integrity of the fund of which he is the trustee.
What I say is this. Under section 20 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, a section which endows these trustees of the fund with full responsibility for all of its investments, there has arisen since this government came into office a situation that did not confront these gentlemen as trustees previously under the former administration. They were not then confronted with a situation in which the government had a large and dangerous deficit. They were not then confronted with a situation that revealed an extremely high level of unemployment making serious drains on the fund. So after this government came into office in the fall of 1958 or, I will say, in the summer of 1958, there arose an extremely important development, a responsibility of which this government should have been aware and which they should have discussed with the members of the investment committee. When the government decided to embark upon its bond conversion scheme there at once arose, as between the governor of the bank and the members of the investment committee as gentlemen responsible in part for the debt management policy of this government, an incompatibility in the face of their responsibility as trustees of the unemployment insurance fund.

Unemployment Insurance Act
This fund is not something that belongs to the government of Canada. This fund is something that belongs to the employers and to the workers of Canada in the main. It is not money that is the property of the people of Canada through the government of the nation. This is property that belongs to the workers and to the employers of the nation. The same regard that one would display with regard to any private trust fund or any private estate must attend the administration of the unemployment insurance fund. I say that there was on this government a responsibility to free the members of the investment committee from the dual position in which they found themselves a few months prior to the introduction of this government's well known, doubtful and controversial bond conversion scheme.
It was in the interests of those responsible for the debt management policy of the government to see to it that the Canadian public were encouraged to invest, or having invested to continue their investment, in long term securities. That was the main characterization of the plan, and inducements were given to those holders of victory bonds to convert their victory bonds into long term securities, characterized by the bond conversion scheme covering some $6 billion, $1 billion of which was held in the hands of private individuals and the rest for the most part by institutions in one way or another.
I say, and in the committee it was so revealed, that it was not in the interests of this fund that the securities of the fund should have been invested in long term securities, and particularly in the bond conversion scheme proposed to this country by the Minister of Finance. I am not now concerned with the merits of the bond conversion scheme, but I am saying that the interests of the government in respect of its debt management policy and the interests of this fund were diametrically opposed. First of all, when the bond conversion scheme was announced the government made it clear that the holders of victory bonds, those bonds which it was encouraging the Canadian public to transfer or to convert into the bond conversion scheme, could be sold on the market, and because the Bank of Canada was supporting that market from July 1958 to the end of October 1958 any seller of those bonds in that period would have received par or its equivalent. The bond market was, as I say, being supported at that time by the Bank of Canada, and if the investment committee of this unemployment insurance fund had decided, to enable those securities to be sold, to take advantage of the market opportunities at the moment, the fund would

have very considerably benefited in the appreciation that would have flowed from that kind of sale. But it was not in the interest of those responsible for the debt management policy of the government to encourage such a sale. There was clearly a conflict of duty between the members of the investment committee, who also had a responsibility as important government officials in the debt management policy of the government.
Is it conceivable that the governor of the Bank of Canada or the deputy minister of finance, in respect of a fund so large, the largest trust fund in the nation, could have taken a step contrary to the admonitions and the urgings of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister of Canada?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And the advice they gave.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
And the advice, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River points out, which they gave to the Canadian public. Of course the members of the investment committee were in a difficult position. They were in a dilemma, and I have no doubt that each of them must have been greatly concerned about the position in which he found himself as a result of the policy of this government. If those five issues of victory bonds held by the unemployment insurance commission, totalling over $300 million, had on a day to day basis-I do not say all at once-been sold on the market, a market which was supported by the Bank of Canada, then instead of reporting now a book loss of $62 million marking the level of the unemployment insurance fund at this time of $350 million, that fund would be up very considerably and would have provided the Minister of Labour with a less justifiable reason for coming to parliament and asking that this fund be replenished by imposing additional burdens on the workers and employers of this country. That is the situation which the facts as revealed in this committee clearly establish.
But they did not sell the victory bonds. They converted these bonds, $380 million worth of them. I say that at that time the interests of the fund demanded it be in liquid state. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the government of Canada must both have known at that time that the unemployment situation in our country demanded that this unemployment insurance fund be in a state of great liquidity. Unemployment was confronting us. It existed all during the summer of 1958 and it was clear from every index that it was going to persist in 1959, as we now know it did in the unusually high proportions that we all saw during the last winter. Because of that condition, does any

hon. member, including the Minister of Labour, care to argue seriously that it was in the interests of the unemployment insurance fund that its securities should be invested in long term instruments at a time when it should be liquid so as to meet the continuous heavy drain imposed upon it as a result of high unemployment in our country?
That is the situation that confronted the investment committee, and I say to the Minister of Labour that he and his colleagues had the responsibility of discussing this with the investment committee, of recognizing the duality of their functions, and saying to the investment committee, "Obviously you are placed in a difficult position; we have no right to ask you to be placed in a position where you have to select between two duties, between two trusts." Under the act as it stood and as it now stands no one else but these three or their nominees could act as members of the investment committee. Parliament was sitting in the summer of 1958. We met here shortly after the elections of March, 1958. There was no reason why the Minister of Labour could not have suggested an amendment to section 20 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and we could have had placed, in the place of these three, three other trustees of competence and of knowledge.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Two others.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Two others, the Department of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada-whose duties as trustees would not have conflicted with their obvious duty to the government and the people of Canada as a whole. Because that was not done, this unemployment insurance investment committee having to make the choice it did, made a choice that was not in the interests of the fund, and it was not in my judgment in full compliance with what one must exact from any one exercising his trust toward a fund of this character. This was a fund in which the over-all concern was what is in the interests of the fund, even if that interest conflicted with policy of the government or with the welfare of the concerns of a wider constituency of the Canadian people.
That is the situation, and because these bonds were converted and they are long term bonds, we are faced with the position as the hon. member for Welland pointed out, that as a result of current market values there is a book loss of at least $62 million. Let no one say that because it is merely a book loss that it is not a serious matter. At any time this fund may have to be liquidated. I would like to ask the Minister of Labour if I am wrong in suggesting that when the government of Canada decided on April 2 to extend
Unemployment Insurance Act for the first time cash loans to the unemployment insurance commission there was not a requisition from the unemployment insurance commission for the sale of certain securities.
I hope the Minister of Labour will deal with that question at some time, because we were informed, with some reluctance by the Minister of Finance, readily by the Minister of Labour, that there had been loans extended under two different orders in council bearing interest at 5 per cent under section 96 of the unemployment insurance act to the unemployment commission. To give some indication that these victory bonds, supported by the Bank of Canada, could have been sold at par and more some time between July and October, I point to the fact that on September 15, 1958 $17 million worth of the same victory bonds which had been converted were sold on the open market at the instance of the Bank of Canada. If it was possible to sell that group-and they were sold, as I indicated, at a profit, because those bonds were at that time being supported by the Bank of Canada-there is no reason why a careful policy of investment during this three-month period should not have seen to it that a larger proportion of these holdings were sold so as to benefit, by way of increased appreciation, the unemployment insurance fund.
Not only that, but at the time just prior to the bond conversion scheme the unemployment insurance fund could have had these securities invested, as did the large insurance companies, in treasury bills, short term securities or something which would yield a principal value close to par, bearing some rate of interest, and certainly producing a revenue greater than was produced in the situation which now confronts us in our analysis of the security position of the unemployment insurance fund. Treasury bills and short term securities would have been more in keeping with the demands, the needs and the problems of the unemployment insurance fund than the purchase of these long term investments.
There was no reason for the investment committee deciding on the course it did simply because it would serve as a means of encouraging the sale of conversion bonds, the prized possession of the Minister of Finance. It was contrary to the interests of the unemployment insurance fund to use this particular investments as a means of trying to encourage a wider participation in the bond conversion scheme of the government of Canada, because, 1 say again, this was a trust fund, and the only consideration should have been the question of what was in the best interest of that fund.

Unemployment Insurance Act
But it was not only in regard to this particular situation that circumstances of this kind arose. We had, in 1958-and this was mentioned yesterday when we were discussing the financing of the Canadian National Railways-another example of this kind. And I may say that when this matter was discussed yesterday I was precluded from pursuing it further because it was argued that it was out of order. I was told I would have to wait until this matter came before this committee. I said that if this was the position I hoped the Minister of Finance would be in the chamber when we discussed this question on the unemployment insurance bill. This was a borrowing on the part of the C.N.R. in January, 1958, with the knowledge and full approval of the Minister of Finance, providing 4 per cent with bonds maturing, I think in 1980.

speechtext: A silly argument.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Someone said: "a silly argument". I hope whoever did so will rise immediately after me and point out where this argument is silly. The investment committee decided to invest $15 million of the securities of the unemployment insurance fund in this $300 million C.N.R. issue. I say to the Minister of Finance, as I said yesterday, that this was a difficult issue. It was not readily accepted by the people of Canada. And it would seem that one of the reasons why unemployment insurance securities were invested in this issue was so as to encourage a wider participation in that issue by the Canadian people, and I think the situation one year later confirms what I have said.

speechtext: What was the reason for those two small amounts?

speechtext: This went into effect on February 28, 1950 which was pretty close to the end of the fiscal year. $1,728,964.94 was carried into the next fiscal year before it was reimbursed to the fund.

speechtext: Would it be fair to say there was just this one large $1 million odd payment, but due to this particular time of year it was spread over into other payments?

That is right.
In other words, there was just the one, single and distinct payment from consolidated revenue into the fund, but due to the fact that it came at a bad bookkeeping time during the year there was a little spread before and afterwards of a few thousand dollars.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Since the hon. gentleman has asked me a question, may I refer to what I said?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: There was no question. I made a statement.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I presume the hon. member wants the full facts. Let us get this straight. As reported at page 3540, my remarks were:
I said that when we invaded the fund for the purpose of providing supplementary benefits we took steps to replenish the fund. That was done in the years 1949-50, 1950-51 and in 1951-52. In 1949-50, vote 585 provided for reimbursement to the fund under section 87(f)(1) of the act in the amount of $1,500,000. The actual expenditure amounted, however, to only $13,425.56. The following year, vote 597 provided for similar purposes the amount of $1,780,000, which was fully expended. In 195152, vote 717 provided for $40,000, of which $35,438.35 was spent.
Now it is not the fault of those who sit on this side of the house if when we were in power unemployment was not as great as it is now under hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East who just spoke introduced something there was not an opportunity to pursue in the committee because,

as I recall it, the information was not available. He asked the Minister of Labour whether or not just prior to the time of the April 2 order in council, under which it was decided to borrow from the government henceforth rather than sell securities on the market, there was a normal monthly requisition from the unemployment insurance commission to the Bank of Canada, their agents, asking them in the forthcoming month to provide to them certain cash funds.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, neither the investment committee nor the unemployment insurance commission conferred with me at all in that regard.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is not the point, Mr. Chairman. The minister is quite familiar with the procedure under which on a monthly basis the unemployment insurance commission indicates by requisition-I believe that is the word-to the Bank of Canada what its cash needs are likely to be in the forthcoming month. The minister knows that I was by no means satisfied that the provisions of section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act had been complied with in the flimsy, informal manner which we heard in the committee was utilized and which resulted in this cabinet decision, not on the part of the unemployment insurance commission, as I gather it, but on the part of the government, and not even the experts in the field, the investment committee, as contemplated in section 20. It was astounding to me to hear that this investment committee composed of the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance and a nominee of the Minister of Labour were not consulted in any way, shape or form in this decision.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What decision?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am just explaining. In this decision to henceforth desist from selling government bonds in the fund but to borrow from the government.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know what transpired in the earlier sittings when the investment committee was present but I do know that I attended with the chief commissioner and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River personally questioned us on that and we gave him information to the effect that the decision was made after consultation with the commission.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is perfectly correct, Mr. Chairman, but I pointed out to the minister at that time, as I have indicated to this Commons committee, that I have very grave doubts concerning whether the language of the statute in section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act was complied with through this informal, flimsy procedure of conversation between the chairman of the 66968-9-305
Unemployment Insurance Act unemployment insurance commission and the Minister of Labour and another conversation which was referred to in the evidence between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour. The language of section 86, subsection 1 of the Unemployment Insurance Act is as follows:
Where the amounts standing to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund in the consolidated revenue fund are not sufficient for the payment of benefits under this act, the Minister of Finance, on the requisition of the commission-
May do such-and-such.
"Requisition" is a formal word. I do not have a dictionary in front of me but there are a great number of lawyers in this house and I think they would question whether or not "requisition" would be satisfied by a mere statement on the part of one member of a board of three, the unemployment insurance commission, to the effect that the minister to whom the board reports engaged in a conversation with him and then in turn that minister had some conversation with the Minister of Finance. This statute says that the direct contact must be from the commission by formal procedure and I believe that "requisition" involves some formality directly from the commission of three to the Minister of Finance. That was not done. A decision was made and the amazing thing is-

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I interrupt at this point to say that it is doubtful that I could convince the hon. member or even endeavour to prove to him that everything was done in the right way. Possibly I should not have entered into the matter at all but I was concerned about the fund just as I am concerned about all the responsibilities I have. Although I have not followed the procedure the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is convinced I should have followed, none the less whatever was done was done in good faith.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, Mr. Chairman, I am not one of those who would ever question the good faith or good intentions of the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But you are.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No, I am not.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You say the whole procedure was wrong.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am saying there is a duty on the part of every member of the cabinet because they are always supported by a great number of legal and other types of advisers to make sure that in matters of consequence of this nature that a statute, a parliamentary direction, is observed in the utmost respect. I say that the language of this statute is very clear.
4804	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act
In examining the members of the commission in the committee we did find that there had been nothing more than a word of mouth conversation on the part of one member of the commission and his minister, the Minister of Labour, that there was some anxiety about these losses.
We have had the evidence that there were capital losses last year of some $10 million. They were also aware, of course, that the market value at about this time in relation to the book value was down by $62 million, as several hon. members have said in this debate. A decision was made of utmost importance. I do not blame anyone for bad faith in this but I do cast blame for not following the procedures parliament lays down. Some decisions are matters of judgment. I know a decision would be taken in good faith and there is no question about that. I have the same feeling with respect to the investment committee. However, I share the views of the hon. member for Essex East when he asserts that when times are difficult for the government and when two members of the investment committee have dual responsibilities and when $8 out of every $10 represents trust funds and not government funds, we should be considering at this time the possibility of relieving admired civil servants or government officials of the type that are on this investment committee of any question about dual responsibility or incompatibility in connection with their investment responsibilities for this fund.
The point I am concerned with at the moment is that a decision was made by order in council on April 2 to desist from selling further of the bonds in the portfolio of the unemployment insurance commission. It is not astonishing to think we have an investment committee in charge of an investment portfolio-even though depleted as it was by $62 million in terms of the market value- still totalling something in excess of $360 million. These were experts, the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance and a third member, a nominee of the Minister of Labour who had been on this committee for almost a year and who presumably had experience, who attended, although I am rather doubtful about how many meetings anybody on the investment committee attended. None the less, certainly two out of the three were experts in the investment field.
We had evidence from the governor of the Bank of Canada before our committee that he was not asked whether or not it was propitious, wise or unwise, to follow the course set out in that order in council. That was a decision made politically by the government. We have no evidence that under 

section 86 there was on the part of those three members of the unemployment insurance commission, acting in concert, acting officially, a decision that the time had come to requisition the Minister of Finance and get from him certain funds on loan rather than by utilization of the capital funds that belonged to the unemployment insurance commission.
I think this has never been cleared up either in the committee or in any explanation we have had subsequently. As far as I know, another usual type of requisition was made by the unemployment insurance commission late in March indicating in the customary way they would need net cash requirements in the month of April of whatever the amount was, perhaps $50 million. This had been the customary procedure, and within a matter of a few days it is the cabinet that decides by order in council, after informal conversation between the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance. Are they the experts in this field? Are they the technicians? They never spoke to the governor of the Bank of Canada about this. Apparently they never consulted the other members of the U.I.C. investment committee with financial long time background, such as the deputy minister of finance, as to what should be done in the interests of the unemployment fund, $8 out of every $10 of which were trust funds from outside government sources. This of course is hindsight and I know the decision that was made was made in good faith. I am challenging the authority for making this decision and the procedure under which the decision was made. I say that the cabinet over rode the statute. It did not consult the investment committee; it did not get from the unemployment insurance commission a requisition. It cannot produce in this house what is called in this section a requisition from the unemployment insurance commission saying that the time had come for the Minister of Finance to do something by loan rather than the regular procedure of liquidating the assets they still had in the fund. I think this has to be answered by the Minister of Labour.
Let me come back to the point I made. They pledged rather than sold, as outlined in the order in council of April 2, some $80 million-plus of 4J per cent conversion loan bonds maturing in 1972 as security for a loan, through the Minister of Finance, upon which the unemployment insurance commission was obliged to pay 5 per cent interest. 1 indicated that hindsight is very easy, and I want to be fair. But the result is they reached this decision without expert advice; they did not consult the investment committee.

We have the evidence of the governor of the Bank of Canada on that. The fact is that market-wise the very securities that were pledged for those loans have in the next seven or eight weeks depreciated further in value beyond the $62 million that was referred to by the hon. member for Essex East, by another $6 million or $7 million. In addition, the unemployment insurance commission, whose funds are 80 per cent trust funds, is obliged to pay 5 per cent on $72 million or $73 million that they have received by loan since April 1 in connection with this order in council.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think this committee and the average member of it-and I include myself as one-surely knows a minimum about business to think that we would expect that if there was an investment committee in which the administration says it has supreme confidence, that no cabinet minister amateurish in big finance or otherwise, in a little conversation with his colleagues would decide on something as momentous as this which has resulted in a $7 million loss in seven weeks, without consultation with someone with experience. In addition, the moneys were trust funds. They were not funds that were contributed to by government departments, although these are still trust funds in that they are contributed to by taxpayers. They were insurance funds $8 out of every $10 of which was contributed by employees and employers.
These informal conversations should be inquired into further by this committee. I
Business of the House
refer to the conversation between the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission and the Minister of Labour and next the conversation of the Minister of Labour with the Minister of Finance, which resulted in this order in council. I suggest this order in council was superimposed beyond the conception of section 86 of the statute, superimposed on the commission which I challenge the minister to suggest did formally requisition and decide that this procedure should take place.
In the statute the onus is upon the commission of three to make a decision of this kind.
I see that it is ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
